cells.tense: The practice is steady and the room is quiet around it, and you are here with it.
cells.act: let one structure collapse that could not hold
cells.ask: Take your hand off the part of your routine you keep propping up by hand, for one week, and leave the space open.
cells.core:
You keep a small light. It doesn't flare and it doesn't need an audience; you sit with the same repetition until it becomes something your hands know. Solitude is what this kind of work asks for rather than a place to hide, and the next step shows itself because the ground under you is honest.

That honesty is what this threshold wants from you now. Somewhere in the routine is a structure that only stands because you keep a hand on it — a step, a way of doing it that stopped carrying anything. You don't need to know what replaces it. Remove your hand from it, clear what it leaves, and stand in the gap for a minute without building. What falls was not carrying weight.
cells.sheetLine: What you're holding up is already down.
cells.verb: keeping a small practice lit through repetition
cells.place: at the threshold where something has to end before anything else can start

cells.tense: The next repetition is already being run in your head before this one has finished.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Pick the practice you're gripping hardest and set it down for one day this week, keeping your hands off it until the day is done.
cells.core:
Practice has turned into a way of staying ahead of something. One more repetition, one more pass of refinement, and it might finally be safe — except the safety doesn't arrive, so the refining continues and the room gets smaller. The being alone stopped being chosen. The grip is doing the work now, not the practice, and the fear of stopping is what keeps it going.

Release can be done on purpose rather than suffered as loss. Pick the piece you're holding tightest and set it down for a stretch you can actually keep — a day, an evening — and stay away, even once the itch arrives. What you're setting down isn't the practice. It's the fear that the practice won't hold you if you stop. Set it down and find out.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping the practice too hard to be held by it.

cells.tense: You used to keep the practice going, and that door is already behind you.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: Show someone just starting the thing you used to practice, and receive what they notice back. Keep no count of who gave more.
cells.core:
There's a practice in you that doesn't run. You know what long attention does from having done it, and it isn't lit here. Picking it up again weighs more than picking it up ever did, so you stand at the edge of it, and the standing has gone on for a stretch.

Effort poured straight into that spot won't light it. A fair trade will. Something in the exchange around this has slipped out of true, and a small one corrects it. Hand what you know to a person beginning the same thing, accept what they see back, and keep no score. You aren't owed an explanation for why it stopped. You're owed a way back in.
cells.sheetLine: The practice doesn't run, and you've stopped expecting it to.

cells.tense: The pen is down and the work is still being done in a room you're not claiming.
cells.act: take the next step with only enough light for that step
cells.ask: Notice a skill people come to you for, then do the smallest next piece of it. No plan past that piece, no label for it.
cells.core:
You get good at things without watching yourself get good at them. At some point the practice became a set of hands that know what they're doing, something other people mention and you don't — a way of working that, in your telling, arrived without effort. The skill is yours. The account of it has been left unsigned.

No one is asking you to claim the whole history. Enough light for one step is enough. Take the next small piece of the work, do it without drawing the step after it first, and let what comes next show itself instead of sketching it out beforehand. The expertise was built in a room you were standing in the entire time. Stand in it once on purpose and put your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: The expertise is yours. You just haven't signed for it.

attempts.check: The record says past experiences made practice feel dangerous; it does not say what happened or who was there, so the Too Little cell locates the person at the threshold without naming a cause. A reader could say the practice is simply uninteresting or that stopping was a choice, and the cell still holds, because it describes the standing-still, not the reason. The ask survives being wrong: trading one small thing still teaches proportion whatever the history. The sentence that serves me more than the person is 'the solitary light has gone out in you' — it sounds like a verdict, so it is cut; the reader gets to keep their own account.
